Publish a supplement site

Source: vignettes/publishing.Rmd
publishing.Rmd

This guide takes you from an empty folder to a published site. GitHub Pages serves the site, and Zenodo archives each GitHub release with a DOI. You do each step once, in this order. A later part gives the rule for rendering again after you change a report.

You need three things: the R console, a web browser, and the Git pane of RStudio or the Source Control view of Positron. Run each code block in the R console. Each step names the folder to run its code in. To run R in the site folder, open the folder as a project in RStudio, or open the folder in Positron. The Git pane and the Source Control view need this. For the R steps alone, setwd() with the path of the folder also works. If you prefer a terminal for git and Quarto, the last part of this guide gives the commands for the same steps.

1. Find missing tools

In the R console, in any folder, install the packages and list the tools:

install.packages(c("pak", "usethis"))
pak::pak("jmgirard/supplement")
supplement::check_tools()

usethis sets up git and GitHub from R. Installing it also installs gitcreds, which stores your GitHub sign-in.

check_tools() reports whether Quarto, knitr, rmarkdown, and git are installed. Install each tool that it reports as missing or too old. A Quarto that it reports as not on the system path is fine: render_supplement() finds it. It also reminds you of the two accounts that you need: a GitHub account and a Zenodo account.

2. Set up git and sign in to GitHub

In the R console, in any folder, give git your name and email address. Git writes them into each commit:

usethis::use_git_config(user.name = "Your Name", user.email = "you@example.com")

Then make a GitHub token, which lets R and git act on your GitHub account. create_github_token() opens GitHub’s page for a new token with the right settings. Click Generate token at the bottom of the page and copy the token. Then run gitcreds_set() and paste the token when it asks:

usethis::create_github_token()
gitcreds::gitcreds_set()

Check the setup:

usethis::git_sitrep()

Under Git global (user), it shows your name and email address. Under GitHub user, it shows <discovered> for the personal access token and your GitHub user name. If it reports a problem, it says what to do.

3. Make the site

Pick a name for the site’s GitHub repository, such as my-supplement. In the R console, in the folder that will hold the site folder, run the code below. Use your GitHub user name for owner:

supplement::create_supplement("my-supplement", repo = "owner/my-supplement")

The function makes the folder my-supplement, the site folder, and copies the template into it. Give the folder the same name as the repository: step 5 names the repository after the folder. The function writes the repository into the GitHub link in _quarto.yml. It also writes the site’s GitHub Pages address, https://owner.github.io/my-supplement/, into the site’s README and into the guide for authors. If the folder already holds a file that the template writes, the function stops and writes nothing.

4. Render the site

In the R console, in the site folder, run:

supplement::render_supplement()

The first render writes .gitignore and README.md, the page for the people who read the site’s repository. The guide for authors is GUIDE.md. The render also writes the site into docs/, the folder that GitHub Pages serves.

5. Make the repository, commit, and push

In the R console, in the site folder, start a git repository:

usethis::use_git()

use_git() adds a few lines to .gitignore and lists the files to commit. When it asks whether it can commit them, choose the answer that means yes. When the site folder is open as a project in RStudio, it then offers to restart RStudio so that the Git pane appears.

Then make the repository on GitHub and push the site to it:

usethis::use_github()

use_github() makes a public repository with the name of the site folder on your GitHub account, pushes the commit, and opens the repository in the browser. It stops if you already have a repository with that name.

6. Serve the site with GitHub Pages

In the R console, in the site folder, turn on GitHub Pages for the docs/ folder of the branch that you pushed:

usethis::use_github_pages(branch = usethis::git_default_branch(), path = "/docs")

If the function stops with a message that the default branch of the local repository and of the remote do not match, wait a minute and run it again. Right after use_github() pushes, GitHub can still report another default branch for a short time. Do not run the function that the message names in that time.

The function prints the site’s address. The site is at https://owner.github.io/my-supplement/, with the owner in lowercase. For a repository named owner.github.io, the site is at https://owner.github.io/. GitHub then builds the site, and the address works when the build ends. The repository’s Settings tab, under Pages, shows the same setting.

7. Turn on Zenodo for the repository

Do this step before your first release. Zenodo archives the new releases of a repository that has its switch on.

  1. Link your Zenodo account to GitHub. On Zenodo, open the profile menu, choose Linked accounts, and click Connect next to GitHub. If you signed up for Zenodo with GitHub, the accounts are already linked. Zenodo’s page Linking accounts shows these settings.
  2. Turn on the switch for the repository. On Zenodo, open the profile menu and choose GitHub. Click Sync now, find the repository, and turn on its switch. Zenodo’s page Enable a repository shows these settings.

8. Replace the template placeholders

The template holds example values. A release stops while any value in items 1 to 4 is in place. Items 5 and 6 do not stop a release, but visitors to the site or the repository see them. In the site folder:

  1. In _supplement.yml, write the paper title, the citation, the contact, and the authors. Leave version and the values under zenodo empty.
  2. In index.qmd, delete the box “Before your first commit”.
  3. In LICENSE.md and LICENSE-CC-BY.md, replace YEAR AUTHORS with the year and the authors.
  4. Replace the example report and data. Add your own with supplement::add_report() and supplement::add_data(). Then delete analyses/example.qmd, its stored output in _freeze/analyses/example/, and its item in the Analyses menu of _quarto.yml. Delete data/example.csv and its entry under data in _supplement.yml.
  5. Delete the example’s figure, figures/bootstrap-means.png.
  6. In README.md, replace the example citation under the title with the paper’s citation.

Then, in the R console in the site folder, render the whole site and look for problems:

supplement::render_supplement()
supplement::check_supplement()

Fix each problem that it prints, render again, and run it again. To also test the web addresses on the site’s pages, which needs a network, run supplement::check_supplement(web_links = TRUE). A row from that test can come from a site that you do not control, such as one that is down. release_supplement() does not run this test, so its rows do not stop a release. If the site uses renv, supplement::check_supplement(renv_lock = TRUE) also compares the R and package versions in the stored output of each report with renv.lock, and gives a "renv-missing" row for each report that attached a package that renv.lock does not name. When renv picks a profile for the site, from RENV_PROFILE or renv/profile, these checks read the profile’s lockfile in place of renv.lock. A release does not run these checks either.

When supplement::check_supplement() with its defaults finds no problem, commit and push in the Git pane. Select every changed file, deleted files included, click Commit, write a message such as “Add the paper and the reports”, and commit. Then click Push.

9. Make the first release

In the R console, in the site folder, run:

supplement::release_supplement("major")

The function runs check_supplement() and stops if it finds a problem. Then it sets the site version to 1.0.0 and writes CITATION.cff and .zenodo.json. It prints the git commands that commit and push the release. Then it prints the address of GitHub’s page for the new release, or, when the origin remote is not a GitHub address, the steps to reach that page. It runs none of the commands and opens no page.

  1. In the Git pane, commit every changed file with the message “Release v1.0.0”, and push. Push before the next step: GitHub makes the tag on the current branch when you publish the release, so a release published before the push tags an older commit.
  2. Open the address that the function printed, such as https://github.com/owner/my-supplement/releases/new?tag=v1.0.0&target=main. The address names the current branch, so the page has the tag v1.0.0 filled in, with that branch as its target. Click Publish release right after the push, because a later push moves the branch.

If the function printed steps in place of an address, follow them: on the repository’s page on GitHub, open Releases, draft a new release, enter v1.0.0 as the tag, pick the branch that the steps name as the target, and publish it.

10. Add the DOIs and render again

After Zenodo archives the release, its Zenodo record has a DOI. In _supplement.yml, under zenodo, write that DOI as version-doi and the address of the record page as archive-url. Zenodo also gives a concept DOI, which names every release of the repository. If you write it as concept-doi, the badge uses it when version-doi is empty. Write each DOI in the form 10.5281/zenodo.1234567.

In the R console, in the site folder, write the DOI into CITATION.cff and render the site:

supplement::write_citation(overwrite = TRUE)
supplement::render_supplement()

Then commit every changed file in the Git pane with a message such as “Add the Zenodo DOIs”, and push. The home page now shows the DOI badge and the download link.

Render again after a report changes

Quarto stores the output of each report in _freeze/, and a full render reuses that output. A full render does not run a report again after you change it. So after a report changes, with the report’s data in place:

  1. Render that report by name, which runs its code again, and then the whole site. For a report in analyses/models.qmd, run in the R console, in the site folder:

    supplement::render_supplement("models")

  2. In the Git pane, commit the changed report with its changed files in _freeze/, docs/, and figures/, and push.

Use a terminal instead

Each step above that uses R for git or Quarto, or the Git pane, has terminal commands. Run them in a terminal, such as the Terminal tab of RStudio or Positron. The rest of each step stays as it is.

For step 2, give git your name and email address:

git config --global user.name "Your Name"
git config --global user.email "you@example.com"

When git push later asks for a password, GitHub refuses your account password. Give a GitHub token instead, made on GitHub’s page Personal access tokens, or set up the Git Credential Manager.

For step 4, and for each full render, run in the site folder:

quarto render

For step 5, make a new public repository on GitHub with the name of the site folder. Do not add a README, a .gitignore, or a license. Then, in the site folder, commit and push, with your user name for owner:

git init
git add -A
git commit -m "Start the site"
git remote add origin https://github.com/owner/my-supplement.git
git push -u origin HEAD

For step 6, on GitHub, open the repository’s Settings tab and click Pages. Under Build and deployment, set Source to Deploy from a branch. Select the branch that you pushed and the /docs folder, and click Save. GitHub’s page Configuring a publishing source for your GitHub Pages site shows these settings.

For each commit and push in the Git pane, run in the site folder:

git add -A
git commit -m "Add the paper and the reports"
git push

For step 9, run the commands that release_supplement() prints in the site folder, then publish the release on GitHub’s page as in step 9.

To render again after a report changes, for a report in analyses/models.qmd, run in the site folder:

quarto render analyses/models.qmd
quarto render
git add analyses/models.qmd _freeze docs figures
git commit -m "Update the models report"
git push

When a path is missing from disk and git tracks no file under it, git add stops and stages nothing. So for a site with no figures/ folder, leave out figures.
